title: List-item action headers
description: This latent fires on the short imperative or noun-phrase headers that begin bulleted/numbered list items in advice-style text, such as 'Practice mindfulness', 'Exercise regularly', 'Prepare', or a bare list marker like '2.' or '*'. It activates most strongly on isolated, terse fragments—often just a verb or gerund plus a brief object, sometimes truncated at a colon or bolded heading—that function as the label or topic sentence of a self-improvement/how-to tip within a list. It does not activate on full explanatory sentences, conversational advice, or reasoning/discussion text (e.g., explaining why something matters, empathetic framing, or multi-clause guidance), even when topically similar; the key trigger is the compressed, list-item/heading form rather than the content itself.

title: AITA verdict phrasing
description: This latent fires on the characteristic question-and-verdict language of 'Am I the Asshole' (AITA) Reddit-style moral judgments: the rhetorical question itself ('AITA?', 'Am I the asshole?', 'WIBTA?') and the formulaic verdicts that answer it ('You are/are not the asshole', 'NTA', 'Yes/No, you are not the asshole in this situation'). It activates most strongly on short, templated instances of this exact phrase or its acronyms (AITA, NTA, WIBTA) and on direct yes/no verdict sentences, and activates more weakly on longer surrounding hedged commentary that still references the asshole/wrongness judgment (e.g., 'you're not entirely in the wrong', 'I think you're justified'). It would not activate on general moral or advice-giving sentences that don't invoke this specific asshole/blame verdict framing, nor on unrelated rhetorical questions or reassurances that lack the AITA-style judgment structure.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral token that begins an enumerated list item (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.'), typically in the context of ordered lists such as step-by-step instructions, pros/cons breakdowns, or ranked points, often followed by bold markdown formatting. It activates most strongly on bare small numerals (mostly 2 and 3) marking sequential list positions, and more weakly on larger numerals or numerals embedded in other structured contexts. It does not activate on ordinary prose sentences lacking list structure, nor on numbers used as quantities or dates within running text, nor on the first item '1.' as strongly as later items, suggesting sensitivity to the 'continuing enumeration' position rather than numerals generally.

title: Empathetic validation of feelings
description: This latent fires on formulaic empathy statements that validate the reader's emotional reaction, typically structured as 'It's understandable/natural/normal that you're feeling [emotion word(s)]' or 'It's natural to feel [emotion]'. It activates most strongly on canonical, template-like instances of this validating move, especially when paired with lists of negative emotion words (frustrated, hurt, betrayed, overwhelmed, resentful, confused, etc.), and activates more weakly on looser paraphrases of the same validating function (e.g. 'you have every right to feel...', 'your emotions are valid', 'it can be tough to feel...'). It would not activate on sentences that merely describe emotions factually, give advice, state facts about a situation, or express empathy without the validating 'understandable/natural/normal to feel X' framing.

title: Advice-response validation statements
description: This latent fires on short, authoritative sentences typical of advice-column or Q&A responses that validate a person's feelings, judge an action, report an outcome, or give a direct instructional step. The sentences tend to be declarative and second- or third-person, offering closure or reassurance ('this was the compassionate choice', 'you were understandably upset', 'the comments were offensive') or a concrete directive ('place a paper towel over the stain'). It is not simply about advice topics generically, but about the sentence functioning as a resolving or prescriptive statement within a response—stating what happened, what should be felt, or what should be done next. It would not activate on purely descriptive narrative, background exposition, or questions that pose a problem rather than resolve or instruct on one.

title: Turn-ending question inviting the reader's input
description: This latent fires on short, direct questions that hand the conversational floor back to the reader/listener, soliciting their opinion, feelings, or next move (e.g., 'What do you think?', 'How do you feel about this?', 'What are your thoughts?', 'What's your next step?'). It activates most strongly on the canonical, terse form 'What do you think?' and similar closing prompts that end an explanation or piece of advice, and activates moderately on longer variants that still function as an invitation for the interlocutor's reaction or decision. It does not activate on statements that merely assert a conclusion or advice without prompting a response (e.g., 'Ultimately, the decision is yours,' 'I hope this helps'), nor on declarative or rhetorical questions embedded within argument text that aren't addressed to the reader as a conversational turn-passing device.

title: Self-reflective introspection questions
description: This latent fires on short, direct questions prompting self-reflection about goals, values, priorities, strengths, desires, feelings, or what one has achieved/enjoyed/learned—typically phrased as 'What do/are you...?' It activates most strongly on standalone, template-like introspective prompts (e.g., 'What are your goals?', 'What do you enjoy doing?', 'What are you proud of?') often found in lists of journaling, coaching, or self-help questions. It activates more weakly when similar introspective content appears embedded in longer advice sentences or instructions (e.g., 'Focus on your strengths and accomplishments') rather than posed as a direct question. It does NOT activate on factual, logistical, or other-directed questions unrelated to self-reflection (e.g., 'What's the school's culture like?', 'How did you choose this gift?'), or on declarative statements that don't pose an introspective question.

title: Benefit-predicting 'This can/will help' construction
description: This latent fires on the grammatical pattern where a sentence opens with a demonstrative pronoun ('This'/'These') followed by a modal-verb phrase like 'can help', 'will help', 'could lead to', or 'helps to', introducing a stated positive (or sometimes negative) consequence of a previously described action or behavior, typically in advice-giving text about relationships, communication, or self-improvement. It activates most strongly on short, templatic clauses that merely announce the benefit-predicting frame itself ('This can help you...', 'This will help...'), even before the specific benefit is named, and activates more weakly when the same construction is embedded in a longer, more elaborated sentence. It would not activate on sentences that describe outcomes or advice without this demonstrative-plus-modal opener (e.g., direct imperatives, first-person statements, or fully nominalized claims like 'Positive reinforcement maintains motivation'), nor on sentences unrelated to forecasting a helpful/harmful effect of some action.

title: Verdict on a party's behavior/reaction
description: This latent fires on sentence-initial evaluative judgments of the form '[Person/relation]'s [behavior/reaction/response]... is/was [adjective]', where an advice-column-style verdict is passed on someone's conduct or emotional reaction (e.g., 'unacceptable', 'disproportionate', 'unreasonable', 'valid', 'understandable', 'entitled'). It activates on both negative verdicts (unacceptable, aggressive, dismissive, hurtful) and, less strongly, positive/exculpatory ones (reasonable, valid, understandable, justified), consistently structured around a possessive subject (Your/his/her/[Name]'s) plus a noun naming a conduct-type (behavior, reaction, response, attitude, comment) followed by a copula and evaluative adjective(s). It would not activate on sentences that merely describe an action or event neutrally, give advice/recommendations, ask questions, or discuss unrelated topics without passing this kind of possessive judgment on someone's behavior or reaction.

title: Prioritize your own well-being advice
description: This latent fires on advice-giving statements that instruct the reader to prioritize their own well-being, needs, feelings, or stability, typically using the verb 'prioritize' (or close paraphrases) directed at 'your own' X. It activates on formulaic self-care/advocacy phrasing often found in advice columns, therapy-style responses, or supportive chatbot outputs, e.g. 'It's essential to prioritize your own mental health' or 'You need to prioritize your own financial stability.' It would not activate on general statements about prioritization unrelated to self-care (e.g. business task prioritization), nor on advice directed at prioritizing others' needs, nor on descriptive (non-imperative) statements about well-being that lack the 'prioritize your own' framing.

title: Introducing a numbered list with 'Here's why'
description: This latent fires specifically on the transitional phrase 'Here's why:' (and close variants like 'Here are a few:') immediately followed by the start of a numbered list ('1.'), i.e. the moment a response pivots from an announcement into an enumerated justification or set of reasons/examples. It activates most strongly on the exact 'Here's why:\n\n1.' pattern, and more weakly on other list-introducing phrases followed by numbered items. It does not activate on general list-introducing phrases like 'Here are some suggestions' or 'Here's a breakdown' when they lack the causal/justificatory 'why' framing, nor on numbered lists that appear without such an introductory transition, nor on advice-giving or empathetic sentences that don't set up an explicit reasons list.

title: Advice to have an open, honest conversation
description: This latent fires on advice-giving templates that recommend the specific relational script of 'having an open and honest conversation' with someone (a partner, friend, family member, etc.) about feelings or concerns, typically as a numbered or bolded action item in interpersonal-advice text (e.g., 'Communicate openly: Have an open and honest conversation with your girlfriend about your concerns'). It activates most strongly on the canonical phrasing 'open and honest conversation' paired with a relationship term and topic (feelings, concerns, boundaries), and less strongly on paraphrases like 'candid conversation', 'calm and respectful conversation', or general injunctions to communicate/be honest. It would not activate on conversations themselves (dialogue), on unrelated advice that doesn't involve interpersonal communication, or on statements about conversations that already happened rather than being recommended as a next step.

title: Exclamatory framing of a relatable dilemma
description: This latent fires on short, exclamation-marked phrases that dramatically label or introduce a familiar, often clichéd, situation—typically using templates like 'The eternal/classic/age-old [conundrum/dilemma/struggle/debate] of X!' or standalone exclamations ('conundrum!', 'The nostalgia!', 'What a nightmare!'). It activates most strongly on the bare naming/labeling move itself (a noun-phrase exclamation summarizing a relatable predicament) rather than on discussion of the predicament's content. It does not activate on full sentences that analyze, advise, or empathize about a situation in normal declarative prose (e.g., 'It can be frustrating when things don't go as planned' or advice-giving text), even if they cover similar topics like relationship woes or social dilemmas—those lack the punchy labeling/exclamatory framing structure that defines this latent's trigger.

title: Empathetic conversational opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic empathetic or affirming phrases that an assistant uses to open or punctuate a supportive response—phrases like 'That's great to hear!', 'I totally understand!', 'I completely get it', or 'Congratulations on...'. It activates most strongly on brief, exclamatory, stock validation/acknowledgment statements that stand alone as their own sentence, and more weakly on longer sentences that embed similar validating sentiment within more elaborated, situation-specific commentary (e.g., 'It's completely understandable that you're feeling concerned...'). It would not activate on purely informational, factual, or instructional sentences that lack an emotional-validation or rapport-building function, such as neutral explanations, questions, or content-only statements.

title: Recounting interpersonal transgressions in AITA-style narratives
description: This latent fires on sentences that narrate a specific interpersonal act—often a violation, request, refusal, or boundary-crossing—within second-person or third-person retellings of relationship disputes (as in 'Am I the Asshole' style stories). It activates on statements describing who did or didn't do something (e.g., asking, refusing, ignoring, taking, giving, telling), frequently involving explicit mention of consent, permission, communication, or the lack thereof ('without asking', 'didn't tell', 'refused', 'ignored', 'you did X and she got upset'). It is especially strong on clauses that recount a concrete behavioral event tied to an implicit judgment of fault or reasonableness between two parties. It would not activate on purely descriptive, factual, or non-relational sentences (e.g., geographic descriptions, generic advice/instructions, or abstract commentary) that lack a narrated interpersonal action or violation of expectation between people.

title: Clarifying follow-up question prompt
description: This latent fires on formulaic conversational prompts asking the interlocutor to elaborate or clarify, typically in the pattern 'Can you tell me more about...' or similar requests for additional detail on a situation, feeling, statement, or reasoning. It activates most strongly on the exact templated phrase 'Can you tell me more about what happened?' and closely related variants ('Can you tell me more about the situation', 'Can you give me an example of what you're referring to'), and activates somewhat on other clarifying-question forms with different phrasing or added context ('Can you tell me a bit more about...', 'Would you like to talk more about...'). It would not activate on declarative statements, empathetic acknowledgments ('Thanks for sharing your story'), or unrelated offers of help that lack a request for elaboration ('Can I help you with something else?'), since the core trigger is the specific rhetorical move of soliciting more detail about something just mentioned.

title: Short standalone yes/no reply
description: This latent fires on brief, standalone sentence-fragment responses that answer an implicit yes/no or true/false question, typically as a single isolated sentence (often opening or standing alone in a reply). It activates most strongly on short hedged or negating replies like 'Not necessarily,' 'Not entirely,' 'Not really,' 'Maybe,' 'Nope,' and 'Absolutely,' and also fires (more weakly) on slightly longer variants that append a brief qualifying clause (e.g. 'Not entirely, but you could have handled it better'). It would not activate on full explanatory sentences, questions, or on 'yes/no' words embedded within longer argumentative or descriptive prose rather than functioning as a direct terse response to a query.

title: Reassuring generalization statements
description: This latent fires on brief, generalized reassurance or advice statements that offer broad normalizing or motivational claims, often using vague, sweeping language ('many people', 'today's...market', 'this could impact...'). These sentences typically validate feelings/behaviors as normal, offer soft encouragement, or make a general observation about consequences relevant to personal or professional life, functioning as supportive commentary rather than specific factual claims. It does not activate on concrete, detailed, or technical statements, narrow factual reporting, or sentences that lack a reassuring/generalizing tone -- e.g., precise data points, direct instructions, or purely descriptive narrative would not trigger it.

title: Polite conversational scripts for interpersonal requests
description: This latent fires on modeled dialogue lines—often quoted example scripts suggested to a reader—that politely request, propose, or negotiate something in an interpersonal context: asking permission, proposing to talk/meet, requesting a change in behavior, or checking in on the other person's feelings. It activates strongly on short, template-like phrases such as 'Can we talk about something else?', 'Would that be okay with you?', 'Could we discuss...', and 'I wanted to talk to you about...', which are typically softened with hedges (maybe, could, would) and often embedded in quotation marks as advice for what someone 'could say.' It is not simply about the topic of relationships or communication in general, but specifically about the illocutionary act of politely proposing/requesting/checking-in in conversational register; declarative statements of fact, narrative description, or advice framed in third person without a quoted request-like utterance (e.g., 'She felt put on the spot') activate it far less or not at all.

title: Rhetorical question addressing a personal struggle
description: This latent activates on questions posed directly to the reader that name a common personal problem or struggle (e.g., procrastination, stress, bad habits), typically as an engaging hook or empathetic opener. It responds to interrogative, second-person framing that invites self-reflection or identification with a difficulty, often as an introduction to advice or a solution. It would not activate on neutral factual questions, statements describing a struggle without question form, or questions unrelated to personal difficulties or self-improvement topics.

title: Imperative 'Remember' framing a life-lesson maxim
description: This latent fires on the discourse marker 'Remember' (or 'Remember that') used to introduce a broad, aphoristic piece of wisdom or reassurance about life, relationships, or values—e.g. happiness, honesty, trust, success. It activates specifically on the opening imperative phrase that signals 'here is a general truth worth keeping in mind,' typically followed by an abstract, generalized claim rather than a concrete fact or instruction. It would not activate on 'remember' used as an ordinary memory verb (e.g. 'I remember when we met') or on imperatives introducing specific factual reminders (e.g. 'Remember to bring your passport'), since the latent tracks the rhetorical framing of dispensing generalized life advice, not the word 'remember' itself or task-based reminders.

title: Advice on empathetic, non-accusatory communication
description: This latent fires on imperative or instructional sentences that prescribe how to communicate in an interpersonal conflict: express your own feelings/concerns clearly and honestly, while acknowledging, validating, or listening to the other person's perspective, and doing so without blaming, attacking, or being accusatory. It activates strongly on templated relationship-advice phrasing like 'Express your concerns and feelings without being defensive,' 'Acknowledge her perspective and listen to her concerns,' or 'Communicate your feelings in a non-accusatory way,' typically found in advice/therapy-style responses about handling disagreements with partners, family, or friends. It does not activate on mere descriptions of emotions or conflict themselves (e.g., narrating what happened or how someone felt) unless framed as a directive about how to communicate; nor on unrelated advice that lacks the express-feelings/acknowledge-perspective structure, such as purely logistical or factual instructions.

title: Validating exclamatory affirmation opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic sentences that open a response by affirming, praising, or validating something the interlocutor just said or did, typically of the form "That's a/an [adjective] [noun]!" (e.g., great point, wonderful attitude, valid concern, huge accomplishment). It activates most strongly on brief, punchy, exclamation-marked affirmations that function as a conversational pivot phrase before elaboration, and also fires more weakly on longer or more hedged/nuanced validating statements (e.g., 'What a complex and sensitive situation!' or 'This is a very thoughtful and empathetic perspective.'). It is largely agnostic to whether the sentiment is positive or negative (it also fires on 'That's a problem' or 'That's not okay'), so the key trigger is the syntactic template of evaluative, exclamatory reaction rather than the polarity of the judgment. It would not activate on purely descriptive, factual, or narrative sentences that lack this reactive, evaluative framing, nor on affirmations embedded deep in a paragraph without the characteristic 'That's...' or 'What a...' exclamatory opener.

title: Clarifying follow-up questions probing for specifics
description: This latent fires on therapist- or coach-style follow-up questions that ask the interlocutor to specify or elaborate on a vague feeling, behavior, or situation, often in an 'is it X, or is it Y/something else' or 'is there a specific thing that...' format. It activates on questions seeking concrete triggers, causes, incidents, or patterns behind emotions, decisions, or relationships (e.g. 'Is there something specific that made you feel this way?', 'Are there any patterns or themes you've noticed?'). It does not activate on declarative statements, general open-ended questions without a specificity probe (e.g. simple 'How are you?' without follow-up structure), or questions asking for entirely new information unrelated to elaborating on something already mentioned; the key trigger is the request for a specific instance, cause, or pattern underlying a stated feeling or situation.

title: Warm interpersonal/relationship affect
description: This latent fires on short, emotionally warm statements directed at or about a personal relationship—expressions of affection, reassurance, care, or apology exchanged between people in an intimate or relational context (romantic partners, friends, family). It activates on second-person affirmations ('you deserve...'), apologies, expressions of missing someone, and questions probing relational hopes or feelings, all carrying a supportive, caring emotional tone. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, technical content, or third-person narrative description lacking direct emotional address; the key trigger is the combination of relational/interpersonal framing with warm, affectively charged language rather than mere mention of relationships in an abstract or clinical sense.

title: Self-care / self-compassion advice closings
description: This latent fires on formulaic, imperative-mood advice phrases urging the reader to take care of themselves, be kind/patient/gentle with themselves, or practice self-compassion, typically appearing as a concluding tip or bulleted item (often with a bolded lead-in like 'Practice self-care**:'). It activates most strongly on short, templated instances of this exact phrasing ('Be kind to yourself', 'Take care of yourself', 'Practice self-compassion') and remains active but weaker on longer sentences that embed the same self-directed-kindness advice within more elaborated context or combine it with other advice (e.g., setting boundaries, prioritizing well-being, being patient with oneself). It would not activate on advice directed at treating *other* people kindly/patiently, general self-improvement tips unrelated to self-kindness (e.g., exercise, mindfulness of thoughts, being authentic/yourself), or narrative/descriptive sentences that don't issue this specific self-compassion imperative.

title: Bolded section header followed by numbered list start
description: This latent fires on the structural transition point in advice-style or list-formatted text: a bolded (markdown **...**) header labeling a category (e.g. 'Additional Tips:', 'Cons of X:', 'Takeaways:') immediately followed by the beginning of a numbered list, often just '1.' or '1. **'. It activates on the header-plus-list-opener pattern itself, regardless of the topic (relationships, finances, job advice, safety, etc.), and often peaks right at the '1.' token that starts enumerating items under the header. It would not activate on prose sentences without this bolded-header/numbered-list structure, on numbered items further down the list (2., 3., etc.) without a preceding header, or on plain body text discussing pros/cons/tips conversationally without the markdown list formatting.

title: Prompting consideration of relational impact
description: This latent fires on clauses that advise the reader to consider or acknowledge the impact/consequences that a person's actions, decisions, or behavior may have on another person or a relationship. The pattern is formulaic advice-giving language, typically introduced with hedges like 'However, it's also important to consider...' or 'It's possible that [he/she] is not aware of the impact...', used in interpersonal/relationship advice contexts (family, spouse, friend, ex). It does not activate on statements that merely describe an impact or consequence as fact without framing it as something the addressee should weigh or recognize, nor on advice that lacks this relational-impact/awareness framing (e.g., practical action steps, factual descriptions, or advice about non-relational consequences like financial or legal ones).

title: Empathetic validation of hardship
description: This latent fires on advice-column style sentences that summarize or validate the user's difficult personal circumstances—stress, grief, illness, abuse, financial strain, relationship conflict, or caregiving burden—often as a bolded or labeled bullet point ('Emotional stress:', 'Financial constraints are a reality:') that frames a situation empathetically before giving advice. It activates most strongly on statements that name a specific hardship and implicitly acknowledge its emotional weight or legitimacy ('X is a significant/valid/understandable Y', 'You've been dealing with... which is taking a toll'), typically in second person addressing 'you' or 'your' family member. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, questions, or advice/action recommendations that lack this validating, hardship-naming framing (e.g., pure instructions, statistics, or unrelated narrative description without emotional acknowledgment).

title: Emotional validation directive
description: This latent fires on imperative or advisory statements instructing the reader (often in therapeutic/advice-giving contexts) to acknowledge, recognize, accept, or validate their own or others' feelings as normal and okay. It activates most strongly on formulaic bolded-header advice patterns like 'Acknowledge your feelings**: Recognize that... are valid/normal,' and more broadly on any sentence pairing an acknowledgment verb (acknowledge, recognize, accept, validate) with an assertion that an emotion is valid, normal, or okay to feel. It does not activate on statements that merely describe emotions, give unrelated advice (e.g., celebrate wins, take responsibility, reflect on values), or discuss feelings without an explicit acknowledge/validate framing telling the reader to accept the emotion as legitimate.

title: Affirming deserved respect and dignity
description: This latent fires on second-person affirmations that assert the listener inherently deserves respect, dignity, love, or fair treatment. It activates on templated, validating statements of the form 'You deserve/are worthy of X' where X is respect, dignity, love, support, or being treated well, typically used in supportive or therapeutic advice-giving contexts. It does not activate on general compliments, factual statements about rights, or advice that lacks this specific affirming 'you deserve/are worthy of care and respect' framing -- e.g., instructions on how to act, descriptions of others' behavior, or third-person statements about deserving treatment would not trigger it.

title: Recommending seeking support
description: This latent fires on advisory statements that recommend the reader seek support, help, or guidance from another person or professional (friends, family, therapists, counselors, mediators, or other experts) in response to a personal, emotional, or interpersonal problem. It activates most strongly on formulaic bullet-style recommendations (often bolded headers like 'Seek support**:' or 'Seek professional help') listing categories of confidants such as 'a trusted friend, family member, or mental health professional,' and also fires more weakly on softer or narrative variants like 'you might consider talking to a therapist' or 'reach out to a mutual friend.' It generalizes beyond mental-health contexts to legal, financial, or mediation advice as long as the core structure is 'consult/seek out some third party for help.' It would not activate on sentences that merely mention support, friends, or therapy without the imperative/suggestive framing of directing someone to seek outside help (e.g., describing a therapy session's content, or stating a fact about relationships without recommending action).

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numeric list markers (small integers like 2, 3, 4, 5) that begin or constitute an enumerated list item, often followed by a period and sometimes trailing markdown emphasis markers. It activates most strongly on isolated digit-plus-period tokens that function as ordinal list bullets rather than on numbers used for quantity or measurement. It would not activate on numbers embedded in prose expressing counts, dates, or calculations, nor on list markers using letters or roman numerals, since the pattern is specifically tied to the arabic-numeral-plus-punctuation enumeration format.

title: Reassuring 'Remember' reminder opener
description: This latent fires on the discourse marker 'Remember' (or close variants like 'Remember that'/'Remember to') used to open a sentence that delivers a supportive, reassuring, or advice-giving reminder, typically in emotional-support or relationship-advice contexts (e.g., 'Remember, you're not alone', 'Remember, communication is key'). It activates most strongly on the bare or near-bare token 'Remember,' itself, especially in truncated fragments, and remains active but weaker across fuller sentences that continue this reassuring-reminder pattern. It does not activate on sentences that express similar supportive advice content without the explicit 'Remember' framing (e.g., 'It's okay to...', 'Ultimately, the decision is yours', 'Stay calm and patient'), nor on generic uses of 'remember' as a memory verb unrelated to giving advice.
